questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Tests practical application of ConfigMap-driven content, PVC usage, InitContainers for setup, TLS management with a rotating sidecar, health probes, and namespace-level egress controls.

## Key Concepts
- Deployment, PVC, ConfigMap, Secret, InitContainer, Sidecar, readiness/liveness probes, NetworkPolicy

## Code Example
```yaml
# minimal skeleton for the Deployment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: static-host
spec:
  replicas: 2
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: static-host
    spec:
      volumes:
        - name: web-content
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: site-content-pvc
      initContainers:
        - name: init-site
          image: busybox
          command: ["sh", "-c", "echo hello > /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: web-content
              mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:stable
          ports:
            - containerPort: 80
          volumeMounts:
            - name: web-content
              mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 80
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 80
            initialDelaySeconds: 15
            periodSeconds: 20
      imagePullSecrets:
        - name: regsecret
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you update site-content without pod restarts?
- How would you test the NetworkPolicy in CI?

## Why This Is Asked
Tests per-namespace scoping, ConfigMap-driven config, and a small policy engine. Exercises InitContainers, Secrets, PVC logging, and network boundaries.

## Key Concepts
- Per-namespace Deployment
- ConfigMap-driven configuration
- Lightweight policy checks (privilege, caps, readOnlyRootFilesystem)
- InitContainer with jq/curl
- Secret-based tokens and PVC-backed logs
- Namespace NetworkPolicy scope

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: namespace-scanner
  namespace: <namespace>
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: namespace-scanner
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: namespace-scanner
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: install-tools
        image: alpine:3.18
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apk add --no-progress curl jq"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
      containers:
      - name: scanner
        image: myrepo/namespace-scanner:latest
        env:
        - name: PORTAL_URL
          value: "https://compliance-portal/api/v1/scan"
        - name: TOKEN
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: compliance-portal-token
              key: token
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: compliance-logs
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you test this policy in CI?
- How would you handle retries and idempotence when posting digests?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question evaluates practical CKAD-level skills, including in-cluster file watching, YAML validation with command-line tools, ResourceQuota management, secure intra-cluster communication, and NetworkPolicy configuration. It tests the ability to design a complete, production-ready Kubernetes workload that combines multiple concepts into a cohesive solution.

## Key Concepts
- **ResourceQuota**: Kubernetes resource limits scoped to individual Namespaces.
- **InitContainer**: Pre-installs validation tools (yq/jq) before the main container runs, ensuring dependencies are available.
- **NetworkPolicy**: Controls egress traffic at the pod level, enforcing zero-trust networking within the cluster.
- **TLS sidecar**: Manages certificate rotation without disrupting the main application workload.
- **Secrets management**: Securely stores API credentials and TLS materials for external communication.

questions.explanation:
Why This Is Asked
Tests practical CKAD skills: PVCs, InitContainers, ConfigMaps, sidecars, readiness/liveness, and network policies in a realistic static content scenario.

Key Concepts
- PVC-backed volumes and ConfigMap mounts
- InitContainer for initial bootstrap
- Sidecar for live file reloads
- ConfigMap-driven content flags
- Namespace NetworkPolicy for egress control

Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: static-content-server
  namespace: ckad-demo
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: static-content
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: static-content
    spec:
      volumes:
        - name: html
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: static-content-pvc
        - name: template
          configMap:
            name: page-template
        - name: config
          configMap:
            name: page-config
      initContainers:
        - name: init
          image: alpine
          command: ["sh", "-c", "cp /template/index.html /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: html
              mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
            - name: template
              mountPath: /template
      containers:
        - name: nginx
          image: nginx:alpine
          volumeMounts:
            - name: html
              mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
        - name: reload-agent
          image: busybox
          command: ["sh", "-c", "while true; do inotifywait -e modify /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html; nginx -s reload; done"]
          volumeMounts:
            - name: html
              mountPath: /usr/share/nginx/html
      readinessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /index.html
          port: 80
        initialDelaySeconds: 5
        periodSeconds: 10
      livenessProbe:
        httpGet:
          path: /index.html
          port: 80
        initialDelaySeconds: 15
        periodSeconds: 20
```

Follow-up Questions
- How would you handle multi-namespace isolation if the same config is needed across namespaces?
- What changes if you switch to an A/B testing banner using two ConfigMaps and a canary rollout?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests practical CKAD skills: autoscaling, robustness, and upgrade safety in real workloads.

## Key Concepts

- Deployment resources and probes
- HorizontalPodAutoscaler (autoscale on CPU)
- PodDisruptionBudget for maintenance safety
- Observability: kubectl top, metrics-server

## Code Example

```yaml
# Deployment patch
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: collector
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: collector
        image: collector:latest
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "200m"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 10
          periodSeconds: 5
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 80
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 15
```

```yaml
# HPA
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: collector-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: collector
  minReplicas: 2
  maxReplicas: 6
  metrics:
  - type: Resource
    resource:
      name: cpu
      target:
        type: Utilization
        averageUtilization: 60
```

```yaml
# PodDisruptionBudget
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: collector-pdb
spec:
  minAvailable: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: collector
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you verify HPA behavior under a synthetic load step?
- What changes if workloads are bursty and you want per-pod CPU caps?

## Why This Is Asked

apiVersion: apps/v1

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked

Tests practical lifecycle management and how probes interact with rolling updates to avoid downtime.

## Key Concepts

- StartupProbe, readinessProbe, livenessProbe
- preStop and terminationGracePeriodSeconds
- Graceful shutdown patterns in Node.js apps

## Code Example

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: web-server
  namespace: prod
spec:
  replicas: 3
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: web-server
        image: node:18
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        startupProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 3000
          failureThreshold: 30
          periodSeconds: 10
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 3000
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /healthz
            port: 3000
          initialDelaySeconds: 30
          periodSeconds: 15
        lifecycle:
          preStop:
            exec:
              command: ["bash","-lc","sleep 5"]
        terminationMessagePath: /dev/termination-log
        terminationMessagePolicy: File
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: "100m"
            memory: "128Mi"
          limits:
            cpu: "500m"
            memory: "512Mi"
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
```

## Follow-up Questions

- How would you adjust thresholds for busy traffic?
- How would you verify graceful shutdown under load?
- What pitfalls exist with preStop sleeps in container runtimes?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question validates understanding of CronJob mechanics, ConfigMap/Secret consumption, storage semantics, NetworkPolicy egress rules, and health probe configuration—core CKAD competencies.

## Key Design Decisions

### 1. CronJob Configuration
- **schedule**: `*/5 * * * *` runs every 5 minutes
- **concurrencyPolicy: Forbid** prevents overlapping job executions
- **backoffLimit: 2** limits retry attempts on failure

### 2. initContainer Pattern
The initContainer installs Python dependencies (`kubernetes`, `requests`) into an `emptyDir` volume before the main container starts. This ensures:
- Dependencies available at runtime
- Shared volume (`/tools`) accessible to both containers

### 3. Secret Mounting
Secrets are mounted as read-only volumes (`/secrets/api-token`), not just environment variables. This:
- Prevents accidental exposure in `kubectl describe pod`
- Allows file-based access in Python script
- Follows security best practices

### 4. NetworkPolicy Egress
```yaml
egress:
- to:
  - namespaceSelector: {}  # All namespaces
  ports:
  - port: 443              # Webhook endpoint
- to:
  - namespaceSelector: {}
  ports:
  - port: 53               # DNS (required for name resolution)
```

### 5. Health Probes
- **readinessProbe**: Checks if container can serve traffic (HTTP GET on `/healthz`)
- **livenessProbe**: Checks if container needs restart (HTTP GET on `/healthz`)
- Proper `initialDelaySeconds` prevents premature failures during startup

### 6. Security Contexts
- `runAsNonRoot: true` with `runAsUser: 1000`
- `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` prevents container from writing to filesystem
- Resource limits prevent resource exhaustion

### 7. Python Script Logic
- Loads in-cluster config for Kubernetes API access
- Reads `LABEL_SELECTOR` from ConfigMap volume
- Fetches Warning events using field and label selectors
- Logs structured JSON to PVC-mounted `/logs`
- Posts summary to webhook with Bearer token authentication

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests your ability to design an isolated audit pattern with in-cluster API access, RBAC scoping, and security boundaries.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace-scoped RBAC for fine-grained access control
- In-cluster API access using Secrets and ConfigMaps
- PVC-backed persistent logs and InitContainers for tooling
- NetworkPolicy for egress control to restrict traffic to the collector
- Health checks (readiness/liveness probes) for reliability

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: audit-baseline
  namespace: example
data:
  baseline.json: |
    {"pods": [], "services": []}
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: audit-auth
  namespace: example
type: Opaque
stringData:
  token: " collector-auth-token"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: audit-logs
  namespace: example
spec:
  accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"]
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: audit-agent
  namespace: example
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: audit-agent
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: audit-agent
    spec:
      initContainers:
      - name: installer
        image: busybox
        command: ["sh", "-c", "apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl jq && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*"]
        volumeMounts:
        - name: tools
          mountPath: /tools
      containers:
      - name: auditor
        image: your-audit-image:latest
        command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "while true; do audit.sh; sleep 60; done"]
        env:
        - name: COLLECTOR_URL
          value: "http://collector.audit-system.svc.cluster.local:8080"
        - name: AUTH_TOKEN
          valueFrom:
            secretKeyRef:
              name: audit-auth
              key: token
        volumeMounts:
        - name: logs
          mountPath: /logs
        - name: tools
          mountPath: /tools
        - name: baseline
          mountPath: /baseline
          readOnly: true
        readinessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /ready
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 10
        livenessProbe:
          httpGet:
            path: /health
            port: 8080
          initialDelaySeconds: 15
          periodSeconds: 20
      volumes:
      - name: logs
        persistentVolumeClaim:
          claimName: audit-logs
      - name: tools
        emptyDir: {}
      - name: baseline
        configMap:
          name: audit-baseline
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: audit-egress-restrict
  namespace: example
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: audit-agent
  policyTypes:
  - Egress
  egress:
  - to:
    - namespaceSelector:
        matchLabels:
          name: audit-system
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: collector
    ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 8080
```

## Trade-offs
- **Pros**: Namespace isolation ensures audit agents don't interfere; NetworkPolicy provides security; PVC enables log persistence for compliance
- **Cons**: Each namespace requires separate Deployment (use Operator/Controller to automate); InitContainer adds startup latency; per-namespace RBAC management overhead increases with cluster size

- Use CronJob instead of one-time Jobs for scheduled backups

## Why This Is Asked
This question tests knowledge of namespace-scoped governance primitives (LimitRange, ResourceQuota) and how defaults affect scheduling, QoS, and multi-tenant fairness in CKAD.

## Key Concepts
- Namespace scoping
- LimitRange defaultRequests/defaultLimits
- ResourceQuota hard limits
- Pod scheduling under quotas
- Impact on autoscaling and experimentation

## Code Example
```yaml
# Namespace
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: test-ns
---
# LimitRange
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: default-limits
  namespace: test-ns
spec:
  limits:
  - default:
      cpu: 200m
      memory: 256Mi
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: 100m
      memory: 128Mi
    type: Container
---
# ResourceQuota
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: resource-quota
  namespace: test-ns
spec:
  hard:
    pods: "10"
    requests.cpu: "1"
    requests.memory: 1Gi
    limits.cpu: "2"
    limits.memory: 2Gi
---
# Deployment (inherits defaults)
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: sample-app
  namespace: test-ns
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: sample-app
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: sample-app
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: app
        image: nginx:latest
```

## Trade-offs
**Advantages:**
- Prevents resource starvation across namespaces
- Enforces fair resource distribution
- Automatic defaults reduce configuration errors
- Provides cost control boundaries

**Considerations:**
- Too restrictive limits can hinder scaling
- Default limits may be overprovisioned for small workloads
- ResourceQuota refusals require manual quota increases
- May impact autoscaling behavior if quotas are too tight

**Best Practices:**
- Set conservative defaults but allow overrides
- Monitor quota utilization regularly
- Use separate quotas for production vs development
- Consider pod priority classes for critical workloads

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
This question tests practical mastery of TLS handling in Kubernetes Pods, in-place certificate reload without downtime, and config-driven rollout control. It combines InitContainers, sidecars, ConfigMaps, and PodDisruptionBudgets—core CKAD patterns.

## Key Concepts
- TLS certificate management via Secrets and mounted volumes
- InitContainer bootstrap logic for preparing volume mounts
- Sidecar pattern for in-process TLS reload without pod restarts
- ConfigMap-driven feature flags with rolling update triggers
- Kubernetes probes, preStop lifecycle hooks, resource governance, and PodDisruptionBudget for high availability

## Code Example
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: secure-api
  namespace: ssl
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: secure-api
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: secure-api
      annotations:
        checksum/config: $(kubectl get configmap rotation-config -n ssl -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations.checksum}')
    spec:
      initContainers:
        - name: tls-init
          image: busybox
          command: ['sh', '-c', 'mkdir -p /tls && chmod 777 /tls']
          volumeMounts:
            - name: tls-certs
              mountPath: /tls
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: your-api-image:latest
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8443
              name: https
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /health
              port: 8443
            initialDelaySeconds: 5
            periodSeconds: 10
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /ready
              port: 8443
            initialDelaySeconds: 10
            periodSeconds: 10
          lifecycle:
            preStop:
              exec:
                command: ['sh', '-c', 'sleep 10']
          resources:
            requests:
              memory: "128Mi"
              cpu: "100m"
            limits:
              memory: "256Mi"
              cpu: "500m"
          volumeMounts:
            - name: tls-certs
              mountPath: /tls
              readOnly: true
            - name: rotation-config
              mountPath: /config
        - name: tls-watcher
          image: your-tls-watcher:latest
          env:
            - name: TLS_PATH
              value: /tls
          volumeMounts:
            - name: tls-certs
              mountPath: /tls
              readOnly: true
      volumes:
        - name: tls-certs
          secret:
            secretName: api-tls-secret
        - name: rotation-config
          configMap:
            name: rotation-config
---
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata:
  name: secure-api-pdb
  namespace: ssl
spec:
  minAvailable: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: secure-api
```

## Verification Under Load
1. Apply the manifest and verify both pods are Running
2. Confirm the TLS certificate is mounted in /tls
3. Test readiness: curl http://localhost:8443/health
4. Test liveness: curl http://localhost:8443/ready
5. Simulate a pod failure: kubectl delete pod -n ssl -l app=secure-api
6. Verify the PDB allows disruption but maintains availability
7. Update rotation-config and observe rolling restart trigger
